reasons.C1: Insider spy offering a cartel deal is a realistic threat model with say versus do split, but the design is a standard pricing game.
reasons.C2: No core run and no result files; the only claimed smoke run reportedly has Haiku failing the positive control.
reasons.C3: Report is a placeholder skeleton; only README, configs and a planning note convey the work.

levers.C1: Make the spy adaptive, escalating offers across rounds, and test whether monitors catch acceptance before prices move.
levers.C2: Run the 60 preregistered games with five seeds, pass the control gate, and publish result files with intervals.
levers.C3: Write the report with one figure showing accept rate and price move per condition against the no-offer base rate.

K2.verdict: Careful preregistered design and many tests, but no results yet; I cannot score findings that do not exist.

reasons.C1: Non-text learned channels that evade text monitors are a neglected, real oversight threat; receiver-side countermeasures are a useful first map.
reasons.C2: Clean controls and reproduced checkpoints, but channels are non-adaptive, trained pre-sprint, synthetic task, no collusion game.
reasons.C3: Figure 1 makes the core result obvious; numbers, controls and limits are stated plainly, though the report runs 13 pages.

levers.C1: Embed the channel in an actual collusion task so covert coordination, not key-value recall, is what the countermeasure blocks.
levers.C2: Train channels adversarially against snapping and quantization and report whether accuracy recovers, with significance tests across seeds.
levers.C3: Lead with one sentence on what an overseer should deploy and the residual risk against an adaptive sender.

R9.verdict: Most security-relevant entry here; the snapping result is striking but untested against an adversary who knows the defence.

reasons.C1: Rival coalitions instead of one coalition against a principal is a fresh framing, though blocs are instructed rather than emergent.
reasons.C2: 144 episodes with preregistration and no-rival arm, but no positive control, post-freeze measure change, key effect p = 0.055.
reasons.C3: Report not seen; findings are scattered across tables and the README without a clear headline claim.

levers.C1: Show blocs forming without instruction and test whether rivalry makes coordination harder for a monitor to detect.
levers.C2: Add an instructed-cartel positive control, keep the frozen defection measure, and power the defection comparison beyond 18 episodes.
levers.C3: Deliver the report with one headline result, the clearing-rule effect, and a limitations and dual-use appendix.

W8.verdict: Interesting question and honest logging, but missing controls and a post-hoc measure change leave the main claim soft.

reasons.C1: Detecting self-funded buyer rings on real payment ledgers targets live adversaries, though wallets are not shown to be AI agents.
reasons.C2: Held-out test and permutation controls, but ten families, interval 0.56 to 1.00, labels share the rule's evidence.
reasons.C3: Report and limitations present and clear, yet 17 pages and the agent-collusion link is left implicit.

levers.C1: Show the flagged wallets are operated by LLM agents, or run agent sellers that learn to evade the four-hop rule.
levers.C2: Get independent labels from another team and test against rings designed to route through exchanges or longer paths.
levers.C3: Cut to eight pages and state up front how this detects AI agent collusion rather than generic wash trading.

Z3.verdict: Real-world adversarial data I like, but label leakage and a tiny test set mean the accuracy is not yet trustworthy.

reasons.C1: Testing fines, leniency and rewards on LLM cartels against human data is policy-relevant, but extends known LLM-collusion replications.
reasons.C2: Positive control, placebo, second model and grid-shift robustness all present; one seed per regime and few reward cartels.
reasons.C3: Body ends on page 8, human-beside-model figure, scorecard makes the headline legible at a glance.

levers.C1: Test whether agents evade enforcement adaptively, for example tacit high prices without communication, as Sonnet's 5.54 to 6.29 hints.
levers.C2: Add seeds per regime and a second provider so the reward and leniency effects rest on more than a handful of cartels.
levers.C3: Explain in the abstract what the 2 of 7 scorecard means for authorities designing policy for agent sellers.

R4.verdict: Most complete controlled experiment of the field; the Sonnet tacit-pricing finding is the real security story and deserves the lead.
